name: Walking speed (usual pace)
summary: How fast you walk at your normal pace over a short, measured distance, in metres per second. It reflects strength, balance and the nervous system working together.
howTo: On a flat, clear floor, mark a start line and a finish line 4 metres apart. Leave at least 1.5 m of free space after the finish so you can keep walking past it.
Stand still with your toes just behind the start line (a standing start).
Walk at your usual speed, 'just as if you were walking down the street to go to the store'. Don't hurry, and keep walking past the finish line.
Have someone time it with a stopwatch: start when the first foot crosses the start line, stop when the first foot crosses the finish line.
Do one practice walk, then one timed walk. Speed = 4 divided by the seconds (for example 4 m in 4.0 s = 1.0 m/s).
If you normally use a stick or walker, use it, and use it the same way every time.
For repeat tests, keep the same distance, start, timing method and shoes. A moving start, a longer course or timing from 'go' give different numbers.
safety: Test on a dry, even, uncluttered floor with good light.
If you are unsteady or have fallen recently, have someone walk beside you.
Stop if you feel dizzy, short of breath, or have chest pain.

norms.label: United States (NIH Toolbox)

source.title: Four-Meter Gait Speed: Normative Values and Reliability Determined for Adults Participating in the NIH Toolbox Study

norms.verifiedFrom: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=6363908&retmode=xml (PMC6363908, author manuscript; Table 1, 'Usual Gait Speed' columns)
norms.population: Community-dwelling adults aged 18–85 from 10 geographically diverse sites in the continental United States, tested August–November 2011 (NIH Toolbox norming phase). 1,320 people (840 women, 480 men), after removing 105 with missing data and 20 with implausible data (a speed under 0.4 m/s, or a usual speed above the maximum speed).
norms.note: 4-metre course, standing start (toes behind the start line), usual pace, keep walking past the finish (a cone at 5.5 m), stopwatch from the first foot crossing the start line to the first foot crossing the finish, one practice walk then one timed walk, comfortable walking shoes. The paper says usual speeds were normally distributed, so it gives mean (SD) and a 95% CI of the mean, no percentiles. SOURCE TYPO: for women 60–69 the printed 95% CI is '1.04–1.02', which can't be right (lower above upper, and it doesn't contain the mean 1.05). It is copied as printed; don't display it, or display only mean and SD for that row. The paper also gives maximum (fast) walking speeds, not copied here. Groups are small (40–223 people), so the band means are imprecise.

evidence.claim: In people aged 65 and older, a slower usual walking speed goes with shorter survival, across the whole range of speeds.
whyThisGrade: Observational: a link, not proof that walking speed itself matters.
Pooled individual data from 9 cohorts (34,485 people aged 65+, followed 6–21 years): each 0.1 m/s faster went with lower risk of death (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.87–0.90), in every cohort.
Meta-analysis of 48 cohorts (101,945 people, mean age 72): each 0.1 m/s slower went with 12% higher risk of death (HR 1.12, 1.09–1.14), but the studies varied a lot (I² 90%).
Earlier meta-analysis: slowest vs fastest quarter HR 2.87 (2.22–3.72), five studies, 14,692 people.
The pooled cohorts were selected studies, mostly from the US and 79.8% white; the authors note healthy-volunteer bias and that the cohorts don't represent everyone.

evidence.claim: Slower walking speed is linked with somewhat more heart and blood-vessel disease in older adults.
whyThisGrade: 13 studies: HR 1.08 (1.03–1.13) per 0.1 m/s slower, with large differences between studies (I² 81%).
A small link, from fewer studies than for death.

studies.title: Association Between Gait Speed With Mortality, Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies

evidence.claim: Walking speed showed no link with cancer.
whyThisGrade: HR 1.00 (0.97–1.04) per 0.1 m/s, consistent across studies (I² 15%), but only in older adults.

studies.title: Objectively measured physical capability levels and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis
Gait speed and survival in older adults

limits: One timed walk is noisy. When the NIH Toolbox group retested people about 9 days later, agreement was only fair (ICC 0.41), and the smallest change that is clearly real was 0.50 m/s, about 45%. Small changes between two tests may be chance.
The result depends on the setup: distance, standing or moving start, timing method, instructions and shoes. Compare only results measured the same way.
Walking speed involves the muscles, nerves, balance, vision, joints and mood. Pain, a recent illness or worry can slow it without any lasting change. It can't say which of these is the reason.
The norms here are from 1,320 adults in the US, with 40–223 people per age band. European norms from a comparable 4 m standing-start test were not found in an open-access source.
The links with survival are from people 65 and older, and from population studies. They describe groups, not what will happen to one person.
